title: Candies
directAnswer: Children stand in a line, each with a rating; every child gets at least one candy, and any child with a strictly higher rating than an immediate neighbour must get more candies than that neighbour. Minimize the total. The trick is two sweeps: left-to-right enforce the 'higher than left neighbour' rule (candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1 when rating[i] > rating[i-1]), then right-to-left enforce the 'higher than right neighbour' rule with a max so you don't break the first pass (candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1) when rating[i] > rating[i+1]). Sum the array. O(n) time, O(n) space.

remember.pattern: Two-pass prefix/suffix DP (left constraint then right constraint, combined with max)
rules: Each child starts at **1** candy — that's the floor every child is guaranteed.
Only a **strictly** higher rating forces more candy. Equal ratings impose **no** constraint, so neighbours with equal ratings can both stay at 1.
The second pass uses **max**, not assignment: `candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1]+1)`. Plain assignment would erase what the left pass earned.
One pass alone is always wrong — left-only ignores right neighbours and vice versa. You need both directions reconciled.
A child sitting at a local peak takes `max(left_run, right_run) + 1`; the two passes deliver exactly that without you computing runs explicitly.
whenToUse: A linear arrangement where each element must beat its neighbour under a local comparison
Constraints point in both directions (left neighbour AND right neighbour) and must be merged
Minimize/assign values subject to 'strictly greater than smaller neighbour' rules
Ratings, heights, or priorities on a line with relative ordering requirements
antiSignals: Comparisons are global (sort-based), not between adjacent elements → sorting / heap, not two sweeps
It's a 2D grid of constraints, not a line → grid DP / BFS relaxation
Equal elements must also differ → the strict-vs-equal rule changes; re-derive
You need the assignment for a cycle (last neighbours first) → relaxation loop, not a clean two-pass
remember.takeaway: When local constraints push from both sides, satisfy each direction in its own sweep and merge with max. Two linear passes beat any single greedy guess and any repeated-relaxation loop — this left-then-right-with-max template solves Candies, Trapping Rain Water's volume idea, and Product of Array Except Self.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that a single greedy sweep can't satisfy constraints coming from both neighbours, and that two directional passes combined with max resolve them in linear time.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Doing only a left-to-right pass (ignores descending runs), or overwriting with assignment in the second pass instead of taking the max — both undercount.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain why one pass fails with a concrete descending example, then derive the two-pass max merge and note the O(1)-space slope-counting alternative.

problemStatement:
Alice is a teacher with `n` students standing in a line, each with a rating. She wants to give candies subject to two rules:

1. Every student must receive **at least one** candy.
2. Any student with a **strictly higher** rating than an immediate neighbour must receive **strictly more** candies than that neighbour.

Given the array of ratings, return the **minimum** total number of candies Alice must distribute.
constraints: Only strictly-greater ratings impose a constraint; equal-rated neighbours are unconstrained relative to each other
Every child receives at least one candy
understanding: Each child has two local obligations: out-rank the left neighbour and out-rank the right neighbour in candies — but only against whichever of them has a strictly lower rating. A naive 'give one more than the bigger neighbour' is circular because that neighbour's count isn't fixed yet. Splitting the obligation into a left-facing pass and a right-facing pass breaks the circularity, and a final max reconciles peaks that must dominate both sides.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If two adjacent children have equal ratings, must their candy counts differ?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The rule fires only on *strictly* higher ratings, so equal-rated neighbours can both hold the minimum. This is the most common misread.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the line circular (does the last child neighbour the first)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, it's a straight line. A circular version would need relaxation until stable rather than a clean two-pass.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need the actual distribution or just the total?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum total here. The two-pass naturally builds a valid per-child assignment, so you can return either.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can ratings be large or repeated?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, up to 10⁹ and repeated freely. Only relative order between adjacent ratings matters, so magnitude is irrelevant.

examples.explanation: Candies [1, 2, 1]. Child 1 out-ranks child 0 (2 > 1) → 2 candies. Child 2 has equal rating to child 1, so it may stay at 1. Total 1+2+1 = 4.
Candies [1, 2, 1, 2, 1]. Each ascending step bumps by one; the equal pair (2,2) and the final drop (3>1) cost only the minimum. Total 7.
Candies [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1] — peaks at indices 1, 3, 7 take more, valleys reset to 1. Total 19.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Repeated Relaxation
approaches.whenToMention: State it to show you can reach correctness mechanically, then replace it with the two-pass once you see the cost.
hints: Start everyone at 1 candy. Now repeatedly scan the line: wherever a child violates a neighbour rule, bump that child up by one.
Keep sweeping until a full pass makes no changes — at that point every constraint holds.
How many sweeps could you need in the worst case? A long descending run like [5,4,3,2,1] propagates one fix per sweep, giving O(n) sweeps × O(n) work.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each sweep is O(n). A monotone run forces the correction to ripple one position per sweep, so up to O(n) sweeps → O(n²) worst case.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct way to *guarantee* a valid distribution: initialise every child to 1 candy, then relax. A relaxation sweep walks the line and, for each child, checks both neighbours: if a child has a strictly higher rating than a neighbour but not strictly more candies, bump it. Repeat sweeps until an entire pass changes nothing.

**Why it converges.** Candy counts only ever increase and the minimum valid assignment is bounded, so the process must stabilise. When a sweep makes zero changes, every local rule is satisfied simultaneously — that's exactly the definition of a valid distribution.

**Why it's not minimal-effort.** Consider a strictly decreasing run `[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]`. The rightmost child is the smallest and needs 1; its left neighbour needs 2, the next 3, and so on — but each sweep can only push the correction one step leftward, because a child can't know its right neighbour's final value until that value settles. So you need ~`n` sweeps, each `O(n)`, giving `O(n²)`. For `n = 10⁵` that's 10¹⁰ operations — far too slow.

**The lesson it teaches.** The reason relaxation is slow is that information from the right propagates left one step at a time. If we instead made *one* dedicated right-to-left pass, that information would travel the whole way in a single sweep. Symmetrically for the left. That observation is precisely the two-pass optimisation.
approaches.insight: Repeated relaxation is slow because constraint information crawls one index per sweep. Giving each direction its own single dedicated sweep lets the information travel the full length at once — turning O(n²) into O(n).

approaches.name: Two-Pass Prefix/Suffix DP (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'one sweep per direction, merged with max'.
hints: Split the obligation in two. First handle only the left neighbour: scan left→right and set candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1 whenever rating[i] > rating[i-1].
Now handle only the right neighbour: scan right→left and require candy[i] > candy[i+1] when rating[i] > rating[i+1].
The second pass must not undo the first — combine with max: candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear passes plus a sum, each O(n), with constant work per element → O(n) time. One auxiliary array of size n → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Break the two-sided constraint into two one-sided constraints, solve each with a single sweep, and reconcile.

**Pass 1 — left to right.** Start every child at 1. Walking rightward, whenever `rating[i] > rating[i-1]`, the child must beat its *left* neighbour: set `candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1`. After this pass, every ascending run is correctly increasing, but descending runs are still flat at the wrong values because we never looked rightward.

**Pass 2 — right to left.** Walking leftward, whenever `rating[i] > rating[i+1]`, the child must beat its *right* neighbour. The candidate value is `candy[i+1] + 1`. But the left pass may already have assigned `candy[i]` a larger value (e.g. at a peak that also dominates its left side). To honour *both* obligations we take the larger: `candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1)`.

**Why the max is the crux.** A peak that is higher than *both* neighbours must exceed both candy counts. The left pass gives it `leftRun + 1`; the right pass would give it `rightRun + 1`. The correct value is the maximum of the two, and assignment (instead of max) in pass 2 would silently discard the left pass's work, breaking ascending runs that feed into the peak.

**Why two passes suffice and are minimal.** After pass 1, the constraint 'greater than smaller left neighbour' holds everywhere. Pass 2's max can only *increase* values, so it never breaks pass 1's guarantees, and it establishes 'greater than smaller right neighbour'. Both rules now hold, and because every increase was forced (each `+1` was the minimum legal bump), the total is minimal.
approaches.insight: A constraint that points in two directions decomposes into two independent one-directional constraints. Solve each in its own linear sweep, then merge with max — the max is what lets a peak satisfy both sides simultaneously without re-running anything.

approaches.name: Slope Counting — O(1) Extra Space
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the space-optimal flourish: count ascending/descending run lengths in a single pass.
hints: Walk once, tracking the length of the current strictly-increasing run (up) and strictly-decreasing run (down).
On a rise, the child gets up+1 candies; on a fall, grow the down run and add it; equal ratings reset both runs to 0 and give 1.
A peak is shared between the up and down slopes — subtract one overlap when the down run grows past the up run so the peak isn't double-counted.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass with constant bookkeeping per element → O(n) time and O(1) extra space (no candy array materialised).
approaches.explanation:
Instead of storing a candy array, accumulate the total directly by tracking slope lengths. Maintain `up` (length of the current ascending run), `down` (length of the current descending run), and `peak` (candies the last peak received).

**On an ascent** (`rating[i] > rating[i-1]`): the run grows, `up++`, reset `down = 0`, the current child gets `up + 1` candies, and remember `peak = up + 1`.

**On a descent** (`rating[i] < rating[i-1]`): `down++`, reset `up = 0`, and add `down` candies for this child. Crucially, when `down` reaches `peak` the descending side has grown as long as the peak's height, so the peak must itself be raised by one — add an extra `+1` to cover that overlap.

**On equal ratings**: both runs reset to 0, the child gets exactly 1.

**Why it's correct.** This reproduces the two-pass result by reasoning about each maximal monotone segment: an up-run of length `k` contributes `1+2+…+(k+1)` style growth, a down-run likewise, and the shared peak is counted once at `max(upLen, downLen)+1`. The peak-overlap correction is the algebraic equivalent of the `max` in the two-pass method.

**Why ship it.** Same `O(n)` time but no auxiliary array — useful when memory is tight. It's trickier to get right (the peak correction is subtle), so reach for the clean two-pass unless O(1) space is explicitly demanded.
approaches.insight: The two-pass max is really comparing the length of the ascending run to the descending run at each peak. Counting those run lengths directly lets you skip the array entirely — the peak gets max(up, down)+1, and everything else telescopes into the running sum.

code.python:
def candies(self, n: int, ratings: list[int]) -> int:
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    total = 1
    up = down = 0
    peak = 1
    for i in range(1, n):
        if ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]:
            up += 1
            down = 0
            peak = up + 1
            total += peak
        elif ratings[i] < ratings[i - 1]:
            up = 0
            down += 1
            total += down + (1 if down >= peak else 0)
        else:
            up = down = 0
            peak = 1
            total += 1
    return total

Ascending run grows; this child's candy and the new peak height are up+1.
Descent adds down candies; once the descent matches the peak, lift the peak by one.
Equal ratings break both runs — this child resets to 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Single-pass greedy
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A left-only pass leaves descending runs flat. On [5,4,3,2,1] it returns all 1s (sum 5) instead of [5,4,3,2,1] (sum 15).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Assignment instead of max in pass 2
commonMistakesDetailed.why: At a peak the left pass earned a large value; plain assignment in pass 2 overwrites it with the smaller right-based value, breaking the ascending run feeding the peak.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (r[i] > r[i + 1]) candy[i] = candy[i + 1] + 1;  // erases left pass

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using >= on equal ratings
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Equal ratings impose no constraint. Bumping on >= over-allocates: [2,2] would cost 3 instead of the correct 2.
